paragraphs.heading: The skin of every cell
paragraphs.text: A lipid bilayer is a thin membrane built from two layers of lipid molecules. Membranes like this wrap around every cell in an unbroken barrier. Nearly all living things, and many viruses, use a lipid bilayer as their cell membrane. The same kind of layer also surrounds the cell nucleus and the other membrane-bound compartments inside the cell.

paragraphs.heading: A wall against water-loving molecules
paragraphs.text: The bilayer's job is to keep ions, proteins and other molecules where they belong and stop them drifting into the wrong places. It is only a few nanometers across, yet it does this well, because most molecules that dissolve easily in water cannot pass through it. Ions in particular are kept out. That lets cells control their salt levels and pH by moving ions across the membrane with proteins called ion pumps.

paragraphs.heading: Heads and tails
paragraphs.text: Most bilayers in living things are made of phospholipids. Each one has a water-loving head, containing phosphate, and a water-fearing tail made of two fatty acid chains. Put phospholipids in water and they arrange themselves into a two-layered sheet on their own, with the tails pointing inward. The result is two leaflets, each one molecule thick. The middle of the sheet holds almost no water and keeps out things that dissolve in water, such as sugars and salts.

paragraphs.heading: Thin but layered
paragraphs.text: The bilayer is extremely thin compared with its width and length. If a typical mammalian cell were blown up to the size of a watermelon, its plasma membrane would be about as thick as a sheet of office paper. Even so, it has distinct zones. The outer head region is fully wet and around 0.8-0.9 nm thick, then a partly wet boundary of about 0.3 nm, then a central core, with almost no water, usually 3-4 nm thick.

paragraphs.heading: Gel or fluid
paragraphs.text: The tails help set how the membrane behaves. At lower temperatures a bilayer can sit in a solid, gel-like state, and at higher temperatures it changes into a fluid one. The chemistry of the tails affects the temperature at which this switch happens. How tightly the lipids pack also affects how well the bilayer resists stretching and bending.

paragraphs.heading: More than lipids
paragraphs.text: Real membranes contain other molecules besides phospholipids. In animal cells, cholesterol is an important one: it strengthens the bilayer and makes it less leaky. Proteins built into the membrane work when they are set into a bilayer. Because the bilayer marks the edge of the cell and its compartments, these proteins take part in many signals passed within and between cells.

paragraphs.heading: Two faces, and fusing
paragraphs.text: The two leaflets often differ. In human red blood cells, the inner leaflet is made mostly of phosphatidylethanolamine, phosphatidylserine and phosphatidylinositol, while the outer leaflet is based on phosphatidylcholine, sphingomyelin and various glycolipids. Some membrane proteins take part in merging two bilayers into one. This fusion plays a part when a sperm fertilizes an egg, and when a virus enters a cell.
